## 

\sectioncardbody{Gold Standard Science?}{}

## 

\darkimageframebody{White House Executive Order}{assets/cgd-opening.png}{https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/restoring-gold-standard-science/}


## What are people concerned about?

Metascience literature has been warning about low standards in research for decades.

My reading of most-cited papers and online discourse:

- Publication bias is rife
- p-hacking is rife (anything can be made significant!)
- "Most published results are false"
- Significant results do not replicate
- Some domains are bad, some are more gold standard
- We should use p-value of 0.01 or 0.001
- Most studies are "cursed" by low power

...plus concerns about data fraud, paper mills, difficulty in publishing nulls, and more.

**Replications** are seen as a diagnostic for most problems above.

## 

\darkimageframebody{Replication are top priority in the NIH GSS list}{assets/nih-tenets.png}{https://www.nih.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/2025-gss.pdf}

## What we learned from systematic replications

\small

- Open Science Collab. 2015: 97 psychology studies reporting significant results
  - **36%** replications statistically significant in the original direction
  - mean effect size fell 50%
- Many Labs 2 (Klein et al 2019)
  - **15/28** statistically significant in the same direction
  - focused on comparing replications across many different groups
  - aimed for high power
  - median effect size fell by 75%
- Camerer et al 2018: 21 social science papers from Nature and Science
  - **13/21** statistically significant in the same direction
  - effect sizes fell by 50%
  - aimed for high power (5x sample sizes)
  - also demonstrated that replications can be predicted
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology
  - low feasibility: **only 1 in 4 experiments could be ran!** 
  - 0/193 had sufficient information to re-run the experiment without help from authors
  - **about half that ran were successes**


## Questions I want to ask in this presentation

- Is there a science-wide "replication crisis"?
- How bad are things currently?
- In which ares?
- What is not working? (which concerns are justfied)
- Of parts that don't work, which can be improved?

I'll try to give a few hints---far from complete picture.


## 

\sectioncardbody{"Trust In Science"?}{Evidence from 100,000 studies}


## Benchmarks of Empirical Accuracy in Research

\small
\textbf{Repository (open source!):} \url{https://github.com/wwiecek/BEAR}

- BEAR is a "meta"-database of $z$-values, effect sizes, and standard errors
  assembled from existing public databases across scientific disciplines.
- Does not contribute new primary data. All credit due to authors of metascience publications and databases from which BEAR pulls.
- Includes millions of $z$-values, including about 100,000 studies from curated datasets.

## We analyse BEAR data in a new statistical modeling paper

"Statistical case for (qualified) scientific optimism", 
with Erik van Zwet (LUMC) and Andrew Gelman (Columbia Uni)

- Input: a set distribution of empirical estimates from papers
- Output: estimates of statistical power, replication probabilities, and more
- Repeat the above for many sets of data
- This part of the presentation is mainly my own interpretation of our (work in progress) paper!




## Two main statistical concepts: z-value and SNR

\small

For study $i$, true effect $\beta_i$:
\[
z_i = \frac{\hat\beta_i}{SE(\hat\beta_i)}, \qquad
\text{SNR}_i = \frac{\beta_i}{SE(\hat\beta_i)}.
\]

Assuming an unbiased estimator with approximately normal sampling error,
\[
z_i = \text{SNR}_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0,1).
\]

Relationship of z to p-values:
$$p = 0.05 \Rightarrow |z| = 1.96, p = 0.01 \Rightarrow |z| = 2.58, p = 0.001 \Rightarrow |z| = 3.29$$



## Empirical estimates "production function"

\small

(We will illustrate this in a moment.)

1. Researchers pick a hypothesis ("draw effect size")
2. Study is designed (fix SE; "aim for 80% power")
3. Therefore SNR is now fixed too
4. Experiment is conducted, adds sampling variation (z = SNR + N(0,1))
5. Researchers may p-hack (move some z-values around)
6. Some non-significant results (p > 0.05, i.e. |z| < 1.96) may go in the file drawer

If we can model distribution of $z$-values, we can model underlying SNR!
If we know SNR, we can derive properties of studies.


## What we estimate

For a study _picked at random_ from a given set:

- **Assurance** (power): probability that $|z| > 1.96$
- **Replication** probability: significant result in the same direction (under same study design)
- **Correct sign** probability: sign($z$) = sign($\beta$)

"picked at random" is a useful concept: should you trust an average study?
can also condition on $|z|$, e.g. "if a study reported $p=0.05$, probability of replication is ..."

## Main results

Across 11 datasets (and various subsets we tested):

- No large discontinuity at |z| = 1.96 _in curated datasets_
- Density decreases in |z|
  - This is crucial: the most common scenario is low power/small effects. 
  - Even in best domains! (e.g. large Phase 3 blinded clinical trials)
  - What differs across domains is width of the distribution
- Expected probability of...
  - ...replication: 20-50% 
  - ...getting the sign right: 70-90%
  - this is for any study (not significant)
- Small proportion of studies reach 80% statistical power (8-29%)


## Small studies are not the main issue

\small

- If you have 5% significance and 80% power, 2x sample size would give you 0.2% significance
  - "aiming for p < 0.002" reform
- But you don't know power in your study!
- Inferred distribution of power in datasets is bimodal. "Good studies" don't need more subjects, "bad studies" don't benefit.
- Impact of doubling all samples: 
  - **replication probability goes from 21-47% to 25-57%**
  - this would still great at decreasing rate of "false positives"

...the issue is that researchers don't have a crystal ball!

## What have we learned?

(my interpretation!)

1. Dichotomisation of results into true and false is a bad model of reality
2. Even worse if dichotomisation is "significant = true"
3. Statistical significance is not a good proxy for strong result
4. Replication rates will likely remain low (significance twice in a row is hard)
5. ... but studies carry useful infrmation!
6. Even a random study highly likely to point in the right direction
7. File drawer problem is less in well-defined research questions
8. Data scraped from PubMed is not fit for assessing empirical research
9. Even best domains (e.g. large scale clinical trials) have same crucial features

## 

\sectioncardbody{You keep using that word...}{A few remarks on replication programs}


## Flavours of replication

\begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
\small

\begin{itemize}
\item "Replication" is not well defined. Three simple distinctions.
\item \textbf{Analytic:} Repeat the analysis using original code and data, e.g. economics.
\item \textbf{Recipe:} Do the experiment, but follow the original protocol as closely as possible, e.g. cancer biology.
\item \textbf{Conceptual:} Test the same claim with updated materials or a new context, e.g. psychology replications.
\item Clemens (2015) counted 41 definitions in social science, most of them about robustness.
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.36\textwidth}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.72\textheight,keepaspectratio]{assets/three_reps_vertical.png}
\end{center}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

## Flavours of replication, cont'd

\small

- Different questions call for different checks
  - Analytic replication checks for basic errors
  - Recipe replication clarifies tacit knowledge/assumptions
  - Conceptual replication help understand external validity
- The boundaries are not clean.
  - Re-running the code but switching to a new implementation of the same method
  - Re-running the same program in the same place, but five years later
- Differences pretty obvious to practicioners & usually easy to choose...
- ...but "failure to replicate" conveys little information

## What counts as failure?

\small

- Failure is sometimes close to binary.
  - If the code does not run, the data cannot be produced, or an image is manipulated, confidence should fall sharply.
- Most empirical disputes are less clean.
  - An original estimate of `d = 0.30, p = 0.001` and a replication estimate of `d = 0.15, p = 0.10` can imply partial corroboration, a smaller effect, or "failure", depending on the rule.
- Significance alone is too crude a standard.
  - Success could mean the same sign, similar magnitude, overlapping uncertainty, or persuasive pooled evidence.
- The useful agenda is broader than "more replications".
  - The goal is to increase confidence in findings that are real and useful, and to discard fragile claims more quickly.

## "Non-replication" without replication

\small

- Not considered replication:
  - Design critique
  - Robustness critique or reanalysis
  - Data provenance / forensic checks
  - Meta-analysis / evidence synthesis
- Important reversals come from post-publication scrutiny
